common_name: Da Hong Pao Tea (Big Red Robe)

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings in spring in acidic, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun; Da Hong Pao Tea is best suited to USDA zones 8-10.

directions: Descended from mother bushes rooted in a rock crevice on Jiulongke cliff in the Wuyi Mountains of Fujian, China, Da Hong Pao is the most storied of the Wuyi rock (yancha) oolong cultivars and today's commercial plantings are cutting-propagated clones of those original plants rather than seedlings. It rewards the mineral-rich, well-drained mountain soils of its native terrain with a deep, roasted character locals call yan yun, or 'rock rhyme,' though growers outside Wuyi can still get a respectable approximation in acidic, humus-rich beds. Give it partial shade and steady moisture, and expect a heavier, slower-growing shrub than the milder green-tea cultivars. Traditional processing involves multiple rounds of charcoal roasting, so leaf destined for this style is usually picked slightly more mature than tea grown for green or white styles.
sources: Tea Research Institute, Chinese Academy of Agricultural Sciences

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings in spring in acidic, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun; Rou Gui Tea is best suited to USDA zones 8-10.

directions: Named for the warm, cinnamon-spice aroma it develops during roasting, Rou Gui originated in the Wuyi Mountains of Fujian, China, and has become one of the two most widely planted Wuyi rock oolong cultivars alongside Shui Xian. It is a vigorous, adaptable shrub that tolerates a somewhat wider range of growing sites than the more finicky heirloom Wuyi cultivars, which has helped it spread well beyond its home cliffs into general commercial plantings. Grow it in acidic, well-drained, humus-rich soil with partial shade and consistent moisture, and prune it into a manageable hedge for repeated hand plucking. Its leaf is typically harvested slightly more mature than delicate green-tea cultivars, since the traditional roasted-oolong process favors sturdier leaf.
sources: Tea Research Institute, Chinese Academy of Agricultural Sciences

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings in spring in acidic, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun; Shui Xian Tea is best suited to USDA zones 8-10.

directions: One of the oldest and most extensively grown cultivars in Fujian, China, Shui Xian is the backbone of both Wuyi rock oolong and the distinct compressed oolong cakes made in Zhangping further south, valued for a soft, orchid-like fragrance that gave rise to its 'narcissus' name. It grows into a notably larger, more sprawling shrub than most named tea cultivars, with bigger leaves that support strong, dependable yields even on modest sites. Plant it in acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade, and give it more room than compact cultivars like Jin Xuan or Tieguanyin. Because it tolerates a fairly wide range of elevations and soils, it is a forgiving choice for growers experimenting with oolong-style processing at home.
sources: Tea Research Institute, Chinese Academy of Agricultural Sciences

common_name: Huang Jin Gui Tea (Golden Osmanthus Oolong)

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings in spring in acidic, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun; Huang Jin Gui Tea is best suited to USDA zones 8-10.

directions: Selected in Anxi County, Fujian, China, and ranked among that region's four historically celebrated oolong cultivars alongside Tieguanyin, Huang Jin Gui takes its 'golden osmanthus' name from an intensely sweet, floral fragrance in the finished tea reminiscent of osmanthus blossoms. It breaks bud notably early in spring compared to most Anxi cultivars, giving growers a jump on the harvest season, and it forms a relatively compact, manageable shrub. Provide the same acidic, well-drained, humus-rich soil and partial shade favored by other Fujian tea cultivars, and pick young flushes promptly once growth begins, since the cultivar's fragrance is most pronounced in the tenderest leaf. Light oolong processing best preserves its floral character.

common_name: Qingxin Tea (Ruan Zhi Oolong, Green Heart)

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings in spring in acidic, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun; Qingxin Tea is best suited to USDA zones 8-10.

directions: Also called Ruan Zhi ('soft stem') or Green Heart, Qingxin is Taiwan's most important high-mountain oolong cultivar and the source of prized styles such as Dong Ding, Alishan, and Lishan oolong, valued for a delicate, creamy, floral cup at elevation. It is less vigorous and more demanding than heavier-yielding modern cultivars like Jin Xuan or Si Ji Chun, growing best on cool, misty high-elevation sites where slow growth concentrates flavor, and it can be more susceptible to leafhopper damage at lower elevations. Plant it in acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade, and expect a more modest yield than sturdier cultivars in exchange for its reputation among Taiwan's finest oolongs. Hand-pluck only the youngest leaves and bud for the best-quality lightly oxidized tea.
sources: Taiwan Tea Research and Extension Station
National Taiwan University Department of Horticulture

common_name: Si Ji Chun Tea (Four Seasons Spring Oolong)

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings in spring in acidic, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun; Si Ji Chun Tea is best suited to USDA zones 8-10.

directions: Selected by a Taiwanese grower and named for its ability to be harvested in four or more flushes a year rather than the one or two typical of finer high-mountain cultivars, Si Ji Chun ('Four Seasons Spring') is prized for vigorous, dependable growth and a strongly floral, almost lily-like aroma. Its heavy-cropping habit makes it a favorite for everyday, affordably priced oolong production, though connoisseurs generally rank its refinement below slower-growing cultivars like Qingxin. Grow it in acidic, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade, and take advantage of its extended harvest window by plucking new flushes as they mature throughout the growing season. It also tolerates lower elevations and warmer conditions better than many prestige Taiwanese cultivars.
sources: Taiwan Tea Research and Extension Station
National Taiwan University Department of Horticulture

common_name: Anji Baicha Tea (Baiye 1, White Leaf No. 1)

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings in spring in acidic, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun; Anji Baicha Tea is best suited to USDA zones 8-10.

directions: Discovered as a chance mutation on a wild tea bush in Anji County, Zhejiang, China, and propagated as the clonal cultivar Baiye 1, this cultivar produces new spring leaves that emerge pale ivory to jade-white because cool temperatures temporarily suppress chlorophyll development, greening up again as the weather warms. That temporary pigment deficiency concentrates unusually high levels of amino acids in the young leaf, giving the resulting green tea, marketed as Anji Baicha, an exceptionally sweet, brothy, umami-rich character prized in the Chinese specialty tea market. Grow it in the same acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil as other tea cultivars, harvesting quickly once the pale spring flush appears since the white-leaf window is brief. It performs best where cool early-spring nights are followed by a gradual warm-up.

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings in spring in acidic, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun; AV2 Tea is best suited to USDA zones 8-10.

directions: Selected as a clonal cultivar for the Darjeeling tea gardens of West Bengal, India, AV2 has become one of the most sought-after cultivars in the region for its ability to produce a pronounced 'muscatel' character, a distinctive grape-like, wine-like aroma most famous in premium second-flush Darjeeling black tea. It is a China-type, small-leaved selection that adapts well to the steep, cool, high-elevation slopes typical of Darjeeling estates, though it can also perform respectably at somewhat lower elevations. Plant it in acidic, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade, and expect a more delicate, slower-establishing plant than robust Assam-type cultivars. Careful withering and oxidation during processing are essential to bring out its signature aromatic profile.
sources: Tea Research Association, Tocklai Tea Research Institute, India
Darjeeling Tea Research and Development Centre
